pending_items.title: Why did Georgian police clash with Turkish football fans over Palestine?
pending_items.content:
Police in Georgia have detained at least 16 people following clashes between football fans at a game between Turkish and Israeli clubs.

The Europa League fifth round match between Turkiye’s Besiktas and Israel’s Hapoel Be’er Sheva was hosted in Georgia instead of Turkiye.

The coastal Georgian city of Batumi was selected last month as a neutral territory to host the game for “safety and security reasons” because of fears of protests over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the European football association, UEFA.

Despite the precaution, tensions between fans spilled over into the stadium and the match was suspended for 30 minutes. Once play resumed, Besiktas won the game 2-1.

It is not the first time violent clashes have marred football matches involving Israeli clubs since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.

Here’s what we know about the latest unrest:

Tensions between fans had already been rising before kickoff in Batumi on Thursday.

According to the Georgian news outlet Civil Georgia, videos on social media showed groups of Besiktas fans marching through Batumi and physical confrontations between fans and police officers.

Turkiye’s Anadolu Agency reported that the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel opposition.

In the 26th minute, the game was temporarily suspended when clashes broke out between Georgian police and Besiktas supporters. Turkish media outlets reported that police entered the stands and used pepper spray against Turkish fans.

According to reports, the police involvement came after a fan displayed a Palestinian flag and banner.

Turkiye’s TRT World reported that police surrounded the fan and used pepper spray, adding that video later showed a Besiktas fan being carried out on a stretcher and others being injured during the intervention.

Omer Celik, spokesperson and deputy chairman of Turkiye’s ruling AK party, posted on X that the “intervention and violence” against the Besiktas fans who unfurled a ‘FREEDOM FOR PALESTINE’ banner and held a Palestine flag was “unacceptable”.

“Besiktas fans spoke on behalf of the alliance of humanity and became the voice of humanity. We strongly condemn the Israeli team’s provocations on the pitch. We extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to our fans who were injured in the incidents and taken to hospital. We are closely monitoring the condition of our citizens,” Celik said.

But Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili told reporters that UEFA officials confiscated the fans’ Palestine flags and Georgian state authorities played no role in the confiscation.

Tamazashvili said that 16 people were detained and three ministry employees injured.

“While marching from European Square towards Batumi Arena, some of the fans of the football club ‘Besiktas’ stood out by their aggressive actions,” the ministry said in a statement.

“They violated the public order by making indecent shouting and shooting of various objects, disobeyed the legal demands of the police, resisted law enforcement and physically confronted them.”

Police took appropriate measures to curb the violence, de-escalate incidents and ensure public safety, including the use of what it called “special means”, the ministry added.

It denied that the use of force was related to the display of pro-Palestine banners and flags.

“We categorically deny this information and emphasise that violent actions by fans and physical confrontation with law enforcers prior to the display of flags and banners have just begun while marching towards the stadium.”

Besiktas said it condemned the use of “disproportionate force”.

“We have initiated formal inquiries with our Consulate General in Batumi and with UEFA regarding the disproportionate force used by security personnel against our supporters; we will continue to monitor the situation closely until every single one of our supporters has returned home safely,” read a club statement.

In a post on X congratulating the Besiktas victory, the Turkish Football Federation said it would “closely monitor the unacceptable behaviour directed at our club, Besiktas and our supporters in Batumi tonight, and that we will take action with the relevant authorities to ensure that these incidents are fully investigated and the necessary steps are taken.”

Other Turkish Super Lig clubs, including Trabzonspor, Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, Erzurumspor, Basaksehir and Samsunspor, also condemned the use of force against Besiktas fans.

Since the onset of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza three years ago, Turkish clubs have not hosted Israeli opposition at home because of security concerns, with matches played in neutral territories instead.

Turkish-Israeli relations have taken a downturn since the war began, with Turkish authorities taking a hard line against the military policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in the occupied Palestinian territories.

However, Georgia and Israel have good relations with close ties maintained amid the war.

Israel’s far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir was in the capital Tbilisi for a diplomatic visit last year.

Last year, English club Aston Villa hosted a Europa League game against Maccabi Tel Aviv , but security concerns prompted West Midlands Police to recommend the banning of Israeli fans from the game.

The decision was taken following violence after a match in Amsterdam between Maccabi and Dutch side Ajax. Police intervened against protesters and Israeli media framed the clashes as a “violent, anti-Semitic pogrom”.

In 2024, another match between Ajax and Maccabi Tel Aviv led to clashes between fans of the Israeli team and pro-Palestine protesters, as Maccabi fans burned Palestinian flags and attacked homes displaying them.

pending_items.title: Evictions and erasure: How Palestinian life in East Jerusalem is being extinguished
pending_items.content:
"The first step in liquidating a people is to erase its memory. Destroy its books, its culture, its history. Then have somebody write new books, manufacture a new culture, invent a new history,” wrote the Czech novelist Milan Kundera.

“Before long that nation will begin to forget what it is and what it was. The world around it will forget even faster.”

Kundera’s subject was Czechoslovakia under Soviet communism. His words also apply to life as it is lived in East Jerusalem today under Israeli occupation. An extinguished city where people live abandoned lives of quiet desperation.

For Palestinians , any form of politics has become dangerous. All political activity - campaign meetings, press conferences, canvassing - is banned and punishable by jail.

The governor of Jerusalem appointed by the Palestinian Authority (PA), Adnan Ghaith, once a busy political activist in the Silwan neighbourhood southeast of the Old City, has been arrested 37 times in his seven years in office.

Symbols of national identity are not allowed. Fly a Palestinian flag and you will be arrested. The national anthem is banned. The authorities search schoolchildren's bags, then confiscate books carrying the PA logo. Shopkeepers in the old city are banned from selling T-shirts with Palestinian national symbols.

I asked a teacher what would happen if he flew the Palestinian flag. “They would close down the school,” he said.

What if he flew the Israeli flag? “They would send me flowers.”

He told me that a school celebration of the national poet Mahmoud Darwish was halted by the authorities.

“We are raising up a peace message in our schools,” he says. “Our only weapon is our books. Why are they treating our schools like this? We are preparing our students to go to university. Not to fight and not to kill.”

On Thursday, Israeli police raided and ordered the closure of Al-Shabat Comprehensive High School, an all girls school in the Wadi Al-Joz neighbourhood east of the Old City, on the grounds that they had found “incitement material”, including Palestinian Authority textbooks.

Israeli activists erase Arabic from street signs. Municipality workers are already taking down signs bearing the name Damascus Gate, in use since the early Ottoman period.

A meeting on Jerusalem’s Mamluk architectural heritage, especially splendid around western entrances to Al-Aqsa in the Old City, was stormed by police earlier this year and the organisers were arrested.

One Palestinian says: “We used to gather, but we are afraid of collaborators. Of private detectives. Of attack.”

Everyone remembers the funeral of Shireen Abu Akleh, the Al Jazeera journalist shot dead by an Israeli soldier while reporting from Jenin in the West Bank in May 2022, when Israeli forces attacked people with batons, causing mourners to drop the coffin on the ground.

So much for freedom of assembly. Freedom of speech is also suppressed. An East Jerusalem head teacher was held in detention during my stay in Jerusalem. She was not calling for violence or even resistance. She had publicly criticised the barbaric treatment endured by Palestinians in Israeli jails, described as “ torture camps ” by the Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem.

Damascus Gate used to be a gathering place for Palestinians. Now it can turn into a place of terror. Palestinians told me that gangs from Lehava, a far-right Jewish supremacist movement whose Hebrew name is an acronym for “Prevention of Assimilation in the Holy Land”, congregate there.

“They start hitting us,” I was told. “Throwing things at us. You cannot respond. If you do, you will be arrested on the spot. Most people go home before 7pm [5pm GMT], when it gets dark.”

In September, an elderly Palestinian, Ahmed al-Husseini, was chased and repeatedly beaten to the ground as he tried to pass through a crowd of men described in Israeli media as “an ultra-Orthodox mob”.

Film of this assault went viral. The person filming the incident was heard declaring in delight: “Wow, they’re fucking up an Arab.”

Israeli security forces standing nearby could be seen looking on without intervening.

Almost all violence goes unreported. Young people are the most vulnerable. A teacher told me his students are regularly assaulted on the way to and from school, and nothing can be done to stop this.

A receptionist in an East Jerusalem hotel frequented by Israelis was attacked by settlers. When she complained, the manager told her to get used to it because it was part of the job.

This account is based on conversations conducted over a three-week period with Palestinians living in occupied East Jerusalem. Some of those interviewed gave permission to quote them by name, but most were reluctant.

I have chosen to leave all interviewees anonymous because it became clear in the course of my research that, for those I spoke to, East Jerusalem has acquired the characteristics of a police state.

Palestinians are subject to ubiquitous surveillance and constant monitoring. Israeli police monitor closed-circuit cameras and use tracking and monitoring tools to join WhatsApp groups and scrape social media content. They also run an extensive, well-developed network of secret informants.

The arbitrary power of the Israeli state has replaced or bypassed every legal or judicial safeguard.

Palestinians live in fear of being hauled into al-Moskobiyya. The notorious Israeli detention facility takes its Arabic name from the local district known as the Russian Compound, which sits just outside the New Gate linking the Old City’s Christian Quarter to West Jerusalem.

During the mandate period, the British held and tortured Jewish prisoners there. More recently, it has become the local headquarters for the Shin Bet, Israel’s security service.

Palestinians speak of abuse inside the jail, recounting stories of sexual humiliation for women and torture (frequently involving anal rape, with sticks) for men.

Accounts of cruelty and torture inflicted on Palestinian detainees in Israeli prisons are taken seriously and documented by Israeli, Palestinian and international human rights groups such as B’Tselem , Addameer and Amnesty International .

“I have never seen my people terrorised like today,” one Palestinian intellectual remarked to me.

He explained that there were, in his view, three reasons for Palestinian political numbness in East Jerusalem.

“First, we have been watching the genocide in Gaza. You can see how Palestinian life is worth nothing to Israel,” he said.

The second factor, he said, was the oppressive presence of the Israeli police. Palestinians suffer grave punishment even for writing a social media post.

“You can be prevented from working, arrested, and imprisoned. Bus drivers have lost their job because of a post years ago.”

The third factor, he continued, is torture: “If you go to prison today, it’s not the same as it was. Nobody gets out of today’s prisons physically and psychologically sound. The levels of torture are beyond all imagination. One month of prison today is worse than several years in prisons in the past.”

He described accounts he had heard of beatings, rape and deprivation, then added: “The International Red Cross is not allowed to visit and we have found that, when lawyers do get access, prisoners beg them not to visit again because after the visit the prison guards beat them up and torture them as punishment.

“So now the only news we get is from those who come out of prison. They come out brutalised. There have been cases where they come out with their anuses so damaged that the bleeding cannot be controlled.”

Israel has barred the International Committee of the Red Cross from visiting Palestinian detainees since October 2023. In September, a Red Cross team met Israeli officials at a military detention facility after Israel’s Supreme Court ruled that its access to detainees should be restored.

The Red Cross called the meeting “a step in the right direction”, but visits to detainees have not resumed.

Occupied by Israel since 1967, East Jerusalem had until quite recently nonetheless sustained a relatively rich civil society with its own history of activism and protest.

Consider the protests five years ago involving sit-ins, neighbourhood gatherings and the raising of Palestinian flags against the expulsion of Palestinians from the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood.

In 2017, Palestinians protested against Israeli plans to install metal detectors around the Al-Aqsa complex by boycotting the site and praying outside. Israeli security forces violently cracked down on the protesters, but the government was forced to withdraw the plans.

That kind of civic resistance has been quashed. I learnt of one senior activist, well known and respected in his professional field, who had recently emerged from an Israeli jail. Because of his political activities, he had been inside prisons often, and had always emerged strong despite the suffering he had endured.

This time, according to a friend who knew him well, he came out broken. He has explained to colleagues that he will never return to political work. He could not endure the same torture again.

Israel is waging a merciless war on Palestinian civil society.

In 2021, several leading Palestinian civil society and human rights groups were proscribed by Israel as terrorist organisations. They included the prisoner support organisation Addameer; human rights group Al-Haq; the Union of Palestinian Women’s Committees; and the Ramallah-based Bisan Center for Research and Development, which helps women who have been victims of violence.
